draft.title: Simultaneous linear equations
card: Two linear equations are simultaneous when we want x and y values that make both true. This is the point where their graphs cross.
Graphing
Draw both lines and read off the point where they intersect.
Substitution
Write one equation as y = ..., then put that into the other equation and solve for x. Then find y.
Elimination
Add or subtract the equations to cancel one variable. Example: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7, and then y = 3.
draft.remember: The solution is the point where both equations are true, which is where the lines cross.

a.q: Solve x + y = 12 and x − y = 2. What is the solution?
a.why: Adding the equations gives 2x = 14, so x = 7. Then y = 12 − 7 = 5. Swapping the values gives x = 5, y = 7, which fails x − y = 2.
a.clue: Add the two equations to cancel y.

b.q: Leo sells mugs in Ballarat. His cost is C = 400 + 5n and his income is R = 13n, where n is the number of mugs. How many mugs give the break-even point?
b.why: Break-even is where cost equals income: 400 + 5n = 13n, so 400 = 8n and n = 50. Check: C = 400 + 250 = 650 and R = 13 × 50 = 650. Dividing 400 by 13 ignores the 5n cost.

proposal.title: Simultaneous linear equations
card: Two linear equations are simultaneous when we want the x and y values that make both true. This is the point where their graphs cross. A break-even point is one such point: where cost equals income, so there is no profit or loss.
Graphing
Draw both lines and read off the point where they intersect.
Substitution
Write one equation as y = ..., then put that into the other equation and solve for x. Then find y. For break-even, set the cost rule equal to the income rule and solve.
Elimination
Add or subtract the equations to cancel one variable. Example: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7, and then y = 3.

final.title: Simultaneous linear equations
card: Two linear equations are simultaneous when we want the \(x\) and \(y\) values that make both true. This is the point where their graphs cross. A break-even point is one such point: where cost equals revenue, so there is no profit or loss.
Graphing

Substitution
